item.title: LDS urges protection of religious freedom

item.content:encoded:
A wakening of constitutional protections for religious freedom could put Fiji’s social harmony, equality and peaceful coexistence at risk.

This was the message from The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS) Pacific Area President, Elder Taniela Wakolo, as he urged the Constitutional Review Commission (CRC) to maintain Fiji as a secular state and preserve constitutional protections for religious freedom.

Elder Wakolo said religious freedom was a right that extended beyond people of faith and applied to every citizen.

He said it included the freedom to worship, the freedom not to worship, and the freedom for people of different beliefs to live together with mutual respect and dignity.

“Fiji’s long history of religious diversity had been one of the nation’s strengths, contributing to social harmony and community service across many generations,” he said.

Elder Wakolo said people from many faith traditions had helped build Fiji by serving their neighbours, strengthening families, caring for vulnerable people and contributing to the nation’s wellbeing.

“Constitutional protections allowing people to live according to their sincerely held beliefs should be carefully preserved because they enabled individuals and communities to contribute freely to the common good.”

He said those protections benefited not only religious organisations but society as a whole.

“The measure of religious freedom is not how well it protects the majority. It is how well it protects everyone.”

He said a just and peaceful society ensured that people of every faith, and those of no faith, were treated equally under the law.

Elder Wakolo said people could hold different beliefs while remaining united as citizens, adding that religious freedom created space for respectful dialogue, cooperation and peaceful coexistence.

He said these principles had served Fiji well and should continue to guide the country’s future.

item.description: A major search and rescue operation is underway in the Lau Waters after six healthcare workers travelling aboard the Ministry of Health and Medical Services vessel, MD Ono-i-Lau, were reported missing while on a medical outreach mission. The team, comprising a Medical Officer, Dental Officer, Charge Nurse, Peer Educator, Health Inspector and Dental Assistant, left Moce at 7am yesterday and was exp
item.content:encoded:
A major search and rescue operation is underway in the Lau Waters after six healthcare workers travelling aboard the Ministry of Health and Medical Services vessel, MD Ono-i-Lau, were reported missing while on a medical outreach mission.

The team, comprising a Medical Officer, Dental Officer, Charge Nurse, Peer Educator, Health Inspector and Dental Assistant, left Moce at 7am yesterday and was expected to reach Oneata after about two hours.

The Ministry of Health confirmed that the vessel’s boat handler was found by a search party from Lakeba this morning and is receiving medical treatment at Lakeba Hospital. The six healthcare workers remain missing.

According to information provided by the boat handler, the vessel’s engine failed before it began taking in water.

The healthcare workers put on life jackets and used the vessel’s wooden floor planks as flotation devices.

The boat handler then swam towards Aiwa Island in an effort to obtain mobile phone reception, leaving the medical team safely secured and without injuries at that time.

When the vessel failed to arrive in Oneata as scheduled, the district nurse alerted Lakeba Sub-Divisional Hospital, prompting the immediate mobilisation of search teams yesterday afternoon.

The Ministry said it had been working closely with the Fiji Police Force, the Fiji Navy Rescue Coordinating Centre, the Office of the Commissioner Eastern and other partner agencies over the past 24 hours.

Command centres have been activated at Lakeba Sub-Divisional Hospital and the Eastern Health Divisional Office to coordinate the emergency response.

Alerts have also been issued to all eight villages in Lakeba, as well as community leaders through district nurses in Nayau, Vanuavatu and Moala, and the Lomaloma medical team.

The Ministry said it had prioritised informing the next of kin of the six healthcare workers and would continue providing updates as more information became available.

It is appealing to seafarers, mariners and coastal communities travelling through the Lakeba–Oneata passage to remain vigilant and report any sightings that may assist search efforts.

item.title: Mother demands accountability
item.description: A Labasa mother is calling for transparency and accountability after her six-year-old daughter suffered a fractured right femur during a school physical education (PE) class. Kartika Chand, 27, of Tuatua, Labasa, said her daughter, Misthi Singh, was injured on June 4 and has since been subjected to weekly medical reviews in Suva.
item.content:encoded:
A Labasa mother is calling for transparency and accountability after her six-year-old daughter suffered a fractured right femur during a school physical education (PE) class.

Kartika Chand, 27, of Tuatua, Labasa, said her daughter, Misthi Singh, was injured on June 4 and has since been subjected to weekly medical reviews in Suva.

“I got a call from her class teacher saying that my daughter got injured but they didn’t tell me how serious it was,” she said.

“When I reached the school, I saw my daughter in severe pain. She couldn’t walk. I took her to Labasa Hospital’s Emergency Department on my own.”

According to Ms Chand, her daughter said she was shoved by another student, causing the injury, and claimed the teacher was not paying attention.

“That is from my daughter’s statement. She also gave the same statement to the police,” Ms Chand said.

Hospital records provided by Ms Chand show Misthi was placed on a 3.5kg skeletal traction for about six weeks at Labasa Hospital instead of undergoing surgery. She underwent repeated X-rays, orthopaedic reviews, pain management and physiotherapy.

However, the family became concerned that the femur was not properly aligned and formally requested the Ministry of Health to intervene for a specialist review.

The six-year-old was subsequently referred to the Colonial War Memorial (CWM) Hospital in Suva for specialist paediatric orthopaedic care.

Ms Chand said she had to take more than a week of unpaid leave to care for her daughter.

“The school gave us $370 as financial assistance. We appreciate it but it does not cover even one month of diapers and wipes, let alone the medical costs,” she said.

“We even had to survive on one meal a day just to manage hospital costs, travel and daily expenses.”

Ms Chand’s account was refuted by the class teacher, who claimed there was adequate supervision during the lesson.

“There was supervision. We had PE class and we were made to run. She ran, slipped and another girl fell on top of her,” the teacher said in a statement.

“She was taken to the classroom, and we applied ice on her right thigh, which was paining. We informed the assistant head teacher and I called the mum. Her grandmother came and they said they will take her to the hospital.”

The school management reiterated that the parents had signed a PE consent form.

“We did sign the PE consent,” Ms Chand said. “But we never signed up for my daughter to go to school and come back with a broken leg. No, that is not why I signed the consent form.”

Education Minister Aseri Radrodro said his ministry did not condone any form of harm to students.

“Please be advised that the MOE (Ministry of Education) has a zero-tolerance policy on student harm and abuse in the school’s vicinity, as articulated in its Child Protection Policy.”

item.title: FCCC seeks powers: Search premises, seize evidence, electronic records
item.description: Under the proposed Fijian Competition and Consumer Commission (FCCC) Bill 2026, the FCCC would be given expanded powers to search premises, seize evidence and access electronic records during investigations. Speaking on the proposed changes, FCCC Manager Legal Krishan Keshwan said during the public consultation on the draft Bill that the existing law only briefly addressed search warrants and lack
item.content:encoded:
Under the proposed Fijian Competition and Consumer Commission (FCCC) Bill 2026, the FCCC would be given expanded powers to search premises, seize evidence and access electronic records during investigations.

Speaking on the proposed changes, FCCC Manager Legal Krishan Keshwan said during the public consultation on the draft Bill that the existing law only briefly addressed search warrants and lacked detailed provisions outlining when they were required and when the commission could instead rely on a requisition for information notice. Mr Keshwan said the commission currently used requisition for information notices to obtain business records from traders believed to possess information relevant to an investigation.

“The notices would inform traders of the information required and are used where the records were expected to be in the trader’s possession,” he said.

“Failure to comply with a requisition for information notice amounts to a criminal breach under Section 119 of the current law, although a defence exists where the information sought is believed to be self-incriminating.”

Mr Keshwan said the proposed Bill introduced an entire division dedicated to search warrants, providing clear legal provisions governing search and seizure powers.

He said the changes were particularly important for digital forensics, where obtaining electronic evidence would require a search warrant issued by a magistrate. Mr Keshwan said applications for search warrants would follow the same procedures prescribed under the Criminal Procedure Act, requiring the Commission to file information outlining the reasons and purpose for the warrant before it was considered by the court.

“Search warrants generally are used to obtain records held by entities that keep information belonging to other people.

“So as such, records can only be disclosed through lawful means.”

Mr Keshwan added that where a trader under active investigation held the records being sought, a requisition for information notice would not be sufficient.

item.title: Be alert, cabbies urged
item.description: Police are urging taxidrivers to seek immediate assistance if they become suspicious of passengers as investigations continue into a series of assaults and robberies targeting drivers, while the Fiji Taxi Association says the attacks have strengthened its push for permanent fare increases and better safety measures. Assistant Commissioner of Police Operations Kasiano Vusonilawe said officers were
item.content:encoded:
Police are urging taxidrivers to seek immediate assistance if they become suspicious of passengers as investigations continue into a series of assaults and robberies targeting drivers, while the Fiji Taxi Association says the attacks have strengthened its push for permanent fare increases and better safety measures.

Assistant Commissioner of Police Operations Kasiano Vusonilawe said officers were doing all they could within existing resources to investigate the incidents and maintain patrols.

“The Fiji police are doing their best in line with the capabilities we have as per investigations and patrols that’s ongoing but we urge the taxidrivers not to be careless and always take precautionary measures that if they are suspicious of their passengers, they can drive first to any police station or community post for the officers on duty to identify their passengers before they continue their journey,” he said.

“For the CCTV issue, we do not have any budget to facilitate all CCTV cameras in every corner of a central business district.”

“In addition, from the month of June alone, we experienced increase in burglary cases compared with the previous months.” Fiji Taxi Association president Mohammed Faiyaz said the recent attacks highlighted the urgent need to improve driver safety.

“The issue is the driver’s safety, we want to put cameras and GPS in the taxi for the safety of the drivers,” he said.

“The drivers don’t deserve to get robbed or assaulted by passengers.”

Mr Faiyaz said the association would seek to make the current temporary taxi fare increase permanent.

“We’ll try to retain this fare, instead of temporary to get the fare fixed.”

Mr Faiyaz called for increased police patrols while urging drivers to remain vigilant when picking up passengers.

item.title: Momi claims under dispute: Landowners refute land swap deal
item.description: Members of the Tokatoka Nahau of Tau Village in Nadroga have refuted claims by Viti Indigenous Tourism Alliance president Sitiveni Nawaqa about the 20-year-old Momi land swap deal. Tokatoka Nahau representative Viliame Tiritiri said Mr Nawaqa did not represent the landowning unit in any discussions regarding their land.
item.content:encoded:
Members of the Tokatoka Nahau of Tau Village in Nadroga have refuted claims by Viti Indigenous Tourism Alliance president Sitiveni Nawaqa about the 20-year-old Momi land swap deal.

Tokatoka Nahau representative Viliame Tiritiri said Mr Nawaqa did not represent the landowning unit in any discussions regarding their land.

“The Tokatoka Nahau is not affiliated with Sitiveni Leseitoga Nawaqa, his company VITA and the vanua Nalolo,” he said.

“Any information regarding Tokatoka Nahau stated by Sitiveni Leseitoga Nawaqa is misleading and at no time have we liaised or engaged his service.”

He said any information regarding Tokatoka Nahau and the land in question, would be given by him on behalf of the tokatoka under the approval of the head of the tokatoka Sokonaia Rogose.

Meanwhile, in response to the concerns by the landowners, Lands Minister Filimoni Vosarogo said the coalition had committed to engaging in dialogue with the landowners.

“The Coalition Government acknowledges the ongoing concerns raised by the traditional landowners of Momi Bay regarding the 2005 land swap associated with the Marriott Hotel development,” Mr Vosarogo said.

“It was subsequently formalised through the Momi Bay Development law in 2010, albeit, by Decree.

“This matter has since become politicised, with the previous FijiFirst Government using it to criticise the decision taken by the Qarase-led Government.

“Our Coalition Government has inherited this complex issue and is determined to approach it with fairness, transparency, and respect for all parties involved.”

item.title: Call to be vigilant, support law enforcement agency
item.description: The growing presence of hard drugs in communities is a threat that cannot be ignored, says Tui Macuata, Ratu Wiliame Katonivere. Ratu Wiliame said reports of methamphetamine and cocaine had become increasingly common in both urban and rural communities.
item.content:encoded:
The growing presence of hard drugs in communities is a threat that cannot be ignored, says Tui Macuata, Ratu Wiliame Katonivere.

Ratu Wiliame said reports of methamphetamine and cocaine had become increasingly common in both urban and rural communities.

“These drugs destroy lives, tear families apart and place our young people at great risk,” he said.

While the Government had established a dedicated task force to strengthen the fight against illegal drugs and related criminal activities, he said the battle could not be won by Government agencies alone.

He said community members had a responsibility to remain vigilant by reporting suspicious behaviour, supporting neighbourhood watch initiatives and looking out for one another.

“Community participation is built on trust, cooperation and shared responsibility.”

He encouraged young people to choose healthy lifestyles and resist harmful influences.

“As the saying goes, it takes a village to raise a child.

“In the same way, it takes an entire community to protect that child and ensure they grow up in a safe and peaceful environment.

He urged everyone to remain vigilant and continue supporting law enforcement agency in addressing crime throughout Fiji.
